name: noScribe
purpose: Desktop application that combines Whisper transcription with pyannote speaker diarisation and ships a built-in transcript editor synchronised to the audio, aimed at qualitative-interview research.
journalism_use_case: Purpose-built for the investigative interview workflow: a long multi-party interview comes out speaker-labelled, and the correction editor lets the reporter verify every quote against the audio before publication — closing the gap between machine transcript and quotable text.
pros: Speaker labelling plus an audio-synced correction editor in one installable app — the combination Buzz lacks and that interview-based reporting actually needs
Designed by a qualitative-research academic, so the assumptions (long recordings, verbatim accuracy, speaker attribution) match investigative interviewing rather than media captioning
Fully local, GPL-3.0, with no cloud option at all — there is no misconfiguration that uploads your interview
Current releases (v0.8, 2026-10-06) and an active repository
cons: CPU transcription of a long interview takes hours; without a GPU the workflow is overnight-batch rather than interactive
Single-maintainer project (2,252 stars, 58 open issues) — the bus factor is one, which matters for a tool in a publication-critical path
pyannote diarisation weights are gated on HuggingFace: you must accept the gate and pre-fetch weights, which both discloses your HuggingFace identity once and complicates air-gapped installation
GPL-3.0 constrains embedding it inside a proprietary newsroom system (not a problem for desktop use)
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented context: the project is explicitly aimed at qualitative social research and is cited in that community; 2,252 stars with 58 open issues. The HuggingFace gating requirement for pyannote weights is documented by pyannote itself and is a known friction point rather than a noScribe defect.
assessment: The better choice than Buzz specifically for interview-driven investigations, because speaker attribution and the verification editor are where quote errors actually occur. For your profile I would deploy noScribe to reporters who do interviews and Buzz to those who process miscellaneous audio, pre-fetching the pyannote weights centrally so individual journalists never need a HuggingFace account — that removes the one privacy wrinkle.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-09, latest release v0.8 (2026-10-06), 2,252 stars, 58 open issues. Regular releases from a single maintainer; activity is current and release-backed.
model_or_data_licence: Whisper weights MIT; pyannote diarisation weights MIT but gated behind a HuggingFace access agreement.
licence_restrictions: GPL-3.0 limits incorporation into closed-source newsroom tooling. The pyannote gate is an access condition, not a use restriction, but it requires an account.
costs: Free. Real cost is wait time on CPU, or one shared GPU workstation. No paid dependencies.
privacy: Local processing with no cloud transcription path — the strongest privacy posture among desktop transcription apps. One-time external touchpoint: accepting the pyannote HuggingFace gate and downloading weights, which can be done once centrally and then distributed internally.
alternatives: Buzz for simpler, faster general transcription without diarisation
WhisperX for engineer-run batch pipelines with the same diarisation stack
Subtitle Edit when the output is captions rather than an interview record

name: NVIDIA NeMo Speech
maintainer: NVIDIA (repository reorganised from NVIDIA/NeMo to NVIDIA-NeMo/Speech)
purpose: Framework for training and running speech models — ASR (Parakeet, Canary), speaker diarisation (Sortformer), speech translation — with pretrained checkpoints distributed via HuggingFace and NVIDIA NGC.
journalism_use_case: High-accuracy English transcription and diarisation at archive scale, and the most realistic route to fine-tuning an ASR model on a dialect, accent or domain jargon that a specific investigation requires — for example months of regional-language broadcast monitoring where Whisper's accuracy is unacceptable.
pros: Parakeet-class models lead open English ASR benchmarks and Sortformer is a genuine step up on diarisation accuracy over pyannote in published evaluations
Fine-tuning is a first-class, documented workflow — the only practical option here if you need a model adapted to a specific accent or vocabulary
Apache-2.0 code with institutional backing and very active development (pushed 2026-11-17, v3.0.0 2026-08-07)
Covers ASR, diarisation and speech translation in one framework, reducing stack sprawl for a speech-heavy newsroom
cons: Checkpoint licences vary and the variation is material: nvidia/parakeet-tdt-0.6b-v2 is CC-BY-4.0 (commercial use allowed) while nvidia/diar_sortformer_4spk-v1 is CC-BY-NC-4.0 (non-commercial only), both read from the HuggingFace cards 2026-11-16 — so the best diarisation model is unusable in commercially published journalism
NVIDIA-GPU-centric: no realistic CPU path, and the dependency stack is heavy
The repository was reorganised (NVIDIA/NeMo now redirects to NVIDIA-NeMo/Speech), so older documentation, pinned paths and tutorials point at the previous structure
462 open issues and a steep learning curve; this is a research framework, not a tool
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented, checkable: the split checkpoint licensing recorded from the HuggingFace model cards (CC-BY-4.0 for parakeet-tdt-0.6b-v2, CC-BY-NC-4.0 for diar_sortformer_4spk-v1); and the repository transfer confirmed via the GitHub API this session. 18,760 stars, 462 open issues.
assessment: Worth it only if speech is central to your work and you have GPU capacity — otherwise faster-whisper plus pyannote is far less effort. The licence asymmetry is the decisive planning fact: you can publish commercially using Parakeet transcription, but not using Sortformer diarisation, so a commercially operated newsroom should pair Parakeet with pyannote rather than taking NeMo's full stack. Fine-tuning capability is the genuine unique value; budget real engineering time for it.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release v3.0.0 (2026-08-07), 18,760 stars, 462 open issues. Daily commits with corporate backing; the repository reorganisation itself indicates active restructuring rather than drift.
model_or_data_licence: VARIES AND MATTERS: nvidia/parakeet-tdt-0.6b-v2 = CC-BY-4.0 (commercial allowed); nvidia/diar_sortformer_4spk-v1 = CC-BY-NC-4.0 (non-commercial only). Read from HuggingFace cards 2026-11-16.
licence_restrictions: CC-BY-NC-4.0 on Sortformer diarisation weights bars use in commercially published journalism unless separately licensed or substituted. Do not assume NGO or non-profit status satisfies NonCommercial — it does not, where the output is commercially published.
costs: No software fee. Requires NVIDIA GPU hardware or cloud GPU rental — the dominant cost, and fine-tuning multiplies it. Checkpoints are free to download. Infrastructure estimate; assumes self-hosted or rented GPU, no vendor licence.
privacy: Local inference and training; checkpoints downloaded from NGC/HuggingFace. No inference-time external calls, so audio stays on your hardware.
alternatives: faster-whisper plus pyannote for a lighter, licence-clean stack
sherpa-onnx for field and offline devices
Whisper large-v3 where fine-tuning is not needed
blockers: CC-BY-NC-4.0 on the Sortformer diarisation checkpoint — commercial-publication blocker for that specific model

name: OCRmyPDF
purpose: Adds a searchable text layer to scanned PDFs using Tesseract while preserving the original page images, with deskewing, cleaning, optimisation and PDF/A output.
journalism_use_case: The standard first pass on a scan dump: makes thousands of image-only PDFs grep-able and ingestable by DocumentCloud, OpenAleph or Datashare while preserving the original page images as evidence — the preservation property is what makes it safe to run across source material.
pros: Preserves the original page image alongside the text layer, so the evidentiary artefact is never replaced by a machine interpretation — the right default for journalism
Idempotent, resumable and designed for batch operation over huge directories; genuinely reliable at scale, which is rare in OCR tooling
Exceptionally well documented and released very frequently (v17.14.2, 2026-11-16) with only 69 open issues against 35,338 stars
PDF/A output and optimisation make the results archive-grade and much smaller, which matters for long-term storage costs
cons: Inherits Tesseract's accuracy ceiling: degraded scans, handwriting and unusual fonts come out poorly and no amount of preprocessing fixes it
Produces a PDF, not structured data — no table extraction, no layout model, so it is the start of a pipeline rather than an answer
MPL-2.0 file-level copyleft is mild but non-zero if you vendor modified source into a proprietary product
Dependency chain (Tesseract, Ghostscript, optional jbig2enc/unpaper) makes reproducible installs fiddly outside containers
feedback: No individual user reports verified. The quantitative evidence is unusually strong: 35,338 stars with 69 open issues and a release on 2026-11-16 — among the healthiest maintenance profiles in the entire catalogue. Widely used as the OCR step in self-hosted document stacks (Paperless-ngx depends on this toolchain).
assessment: Adopt without reservation as the default OCR step for scanned material. Its value for your work is not accuracy — that is Tesseract's limit — but operational reliability and evidentiary integrity: it will finish a 200,000-page job and the originals will still be there. Where accuracy is insufficient, escalate specific documents to Surya/Marker or Kraken rather than changing the default.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-16, latest release v17.14.2 (2026-11-16), 35,338 stars, 69 open issues. Same-day push and release, major version 17, minimal backlog — maintenance quality is evidenced by issue throughput, not just commit frequency.
model_or_data_licence: n/a (Tesseract traineddata is separately licensed, generally Apache-2.0 from the tesseract-ocr project).
licence_restrictions: MPL-2.0 file-level copyleft: modifications to OCRmyPDF's own files must be shared if distributed. Ghostscript is a runtime dependency with AGPL terms from Artifex absent a commercial licence — relevant only if you redistribute a bundle.
costs: No fee. CPU-bound; OCR time is roughly linear in page count, so a large scan dump is a compute-hours cost on commodity hardware. Containerised deployment keeps operating effort low. Estimate.
privacy: Fully local, no network calls, no telemetry. Safe on an air-gapped evidence machine.
alternatives: Surya or Marker where Tesseract's accuracy is the binding constraint
PaddleOCR for CJK and Arabic scans
Dangerzone first, if the PDFs come from an untrusted source

name: olmOCR
purpose: Vision-language-model pipeline for linearising PDFs into clean text with correct reading order, fine-tuned from Qwen2.5-VL and distributed with open weights plus a batch inference toolkit.
journalism_use_case: Genuinely open-weights VLM OCR — rare in this category — so a newsroom can run state-of-the-art document linearisation on its own GPU with no licence threshold and no vendor seeing the documents. The practical use is converting large scanned report archives into reliable text where Tesseract garbles multi-column layout.
pros: Apache-2.0 weights (allenai/olmOCR-2-7B-1025 HuggingFace card) — the only VLM-OCR option here without an OpenRAIL-M or revenue-threshold condition, which makes it the licence-safe high-accuracy choice
Reading-order linearisation is the specific strength: multi-column reports and footnote-heavy documents come out in the order a human would read them
Published with a documented evaluation methodology by a research institute, so quality claims are traceable rather than marketing
Batch toolkit is designed for corpus-scale processing, not single-document demos
cons: No repository activity since 2026-03-25 — nine months quiet, so the current release should be treated as a snapshot rather than a maintained product
Requires a sizeable NVIDIA GPU with vLLM or SGLang; not laptop-viable, which excludes it from reporter-facing workflows
Fine-tuned from Qwen2.5-VL, so Qwen's terms also apply to the derived weights, and AI2 frames use under its Responsible Use Guidelines — a soft-law layer above the Apache-2.0 label
VLM OCR can hallucinate plausible text where the image is unreadable, which is a more dangerous failure mode than Tesseract's obvious garbage
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: 19,829 stars and 93 open issues indicate strong initial adoption; the nine-month commit gap since 2026-03-25 is the key checkable maintenance fact. AI2's published evaluation is a project claim with methodology disclosed, not independent verification.
assessment: Attractive on licensing and quality but the maintenance gap makes it a conditional choice: I would use it for a defined batch job on a specific archive, pinning the release, rather than building a standing pipeline on it. For your profile the Apache-2.0 weights are the reason to prefer it over Marker when your organisation exceeds Datalab's threshold. Add a verification step — VLM hallucination means a spot-check protocol against page images is mandatory before any extracted text is quoted.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-03-25, latest release v0.4.27 (2026-03-12), 19,829 stars, 93 open issues. No commits for nearly nine months against substantial adoption and an open backlog. Classified declining rather than dormant because the project is recent and institutionally owned, but there is no evidence of ongoing work and no deprecation statement either way.
model_or_data_licence: Apache-2.0 on the HuggingFace card for allenai/olmOCR-2-7B-1025; fine-tuned from Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct, so Qwen's terms also apply to derivatives. AI2 additionally frames use under its Responsible Use Guidelines.
licence_restrictions: No revenue threshold or NC clause found. Residual complexity: the base-model terms flow through, and AI2's guidelines are stated expectations rather than licence conditions.
costs: No fee. Requires a GPU host (24GB+ VRAM class for the 7B model with vLLM) — the dominant cost, whether owned or rented. Weights are free. Infrastructure estimate; assumes self-hosted GPU.
privacy: Local inference once weights are downloaded; no external calls. Fully compatible with an isolated processing environment, which is its main advantage over hosted document AI.
alternatives: Docling for a maintained, licence-clean, CPU-viable alternative
Marker for higher accuracy if the Datalab weights threshold is acceptable
Surya for the layout/OCR models without a full VLM
blockers: No repository activity since March 2026 — do not build a long-lived pipeline on it without accepting fork responsibility

name: OpenAleph
maintainer: DARC — Data and Research Center (independent fork of alephdata/aleph)
purpose: Self-hosted investigative data platform that indexes documents and structured datasets as FollowTheMoney entities, provides full-text and entity search, cross-referencing between datasets, and collaborative collections.
journalism_use_case: The primary live candidate for standing up a searchable archive over a multi-million-document leak for a reporting team, with automatic cross-referencing of names in the leak against sanctions lists, PEP data and corporate registries — the capability that turns a document archive into an investigative lead generator.
pros: Cross-referencing across datasets is the distinguishing capability in this pillar: upload a leak and it tells you which names also appear in sanctions or registry data you have loaded

Verified as the actively maintained path: GitHub API confirms fork=true with parent alephdata/aleph, and OpenAleph released 5.4.0 on 2026-11-16 while upstream Aleph last released 4.1.7 in October 2025
MIT licensed, fully self-hostable, with no third-party calls required for core indexing — correct architecture for sensitive material
Maintained in step with its own ingest stack (openaleph/ingest-file) and the FtM/OpenSanctions ecosystem, so the components are version-coherent
cons: Heavy infrastructure footprint: Elasticsearch, PostgreSQL, Redis and worker containers — the highest operational burden of any tool in this segment, and Elasticsearch index sizing is the main scaling cost at multi-million-document scale

Smaller maintainer base than OCCRP-era Aleph (156 stars, 16 open issues) — institutionally backed by DARC but the contributor pool is thin, which is a continuity risk for a system holding your archive
Upgrades across a forked lineage require care; you are now on DARC's release train, not OCCRP's
Reporter-facing UX is functional rather than polished compared with Datashare
feedback: No individual user reports verified. The decisive documented finding, established in this session: GitHub API reports openaleph/openaleph as fork=true with parent=alephdata/aleph, releasing 5.4.0 on 2026-11-16, while alephdata/aleph last pushed 2026-02-20 with release 4.1.7 (2025-10-27). This confirms the fork is the maintained path and the two are not interchangeable (recorded in sources/evidence/leads.md).
assessment: If your work is entity-centric — ownership structures, sanctions exposure, cross-border networks — this is the platform I would build on, and the fork question is now settled in its favour. The honest caveat is operational: do not adopt OpenAleph without someone who can run Elasticsearch properly, because a badly operated index over your only copy of a leak is a serious risk. For a document-centric team without that capacity, Datashare desktop is the better answer.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, fork=true (parent alephdata/aleph), pushed_at 2026-11-16, latest release 5.4.0 (2026-11-16), 156 stars, 16 open issues. Same-day push and release on a 5.x line, with coordinated releases across openaleph/ingest-file. Active and institutionally maintained; small contributor base is the residual risk.
model_or_data_licence: n/a. Datasets you load carry their own licences — notably OpenSanctions data is CC-BY-NC-4.0.
licence_restrictions: Code unrestricted. The licence risk sits in the data you ingest, not the platform.
costs: No software fee. Infrastructure estimate for a few million documents: an Elasticsearch cluster (start at 2 nodes, 16-32GB RAM each), PostgreSQL, Redis, and worker containers for ingest/OCR — realistically a four-figure annual cloud bill or equivalent on-prem hardware, plus meaningful ops time. Assumptions: self-managed Elasticsearch, no managed service, OCR load moderate. The largest cost in the whole catalogue after human labour.
privacy: Fully self-hosted with no third-party calls required for core indexing. Residual risks are operational and serious: the Elasticsearch index must never be exposed, backups contain the entire leak and need encryption, and access control within collections is your responsibility.
alternatives: ICIJ Datashare where a reporter-facing UI and lower ops burden matter more than cross-referencing
alephdata/aleph — reference only; use OpenAleph instead
Uwazi for public-facing collections rather than internal investigation

name: OpenRefine
maintainer: OpenRefine community (Code for Science & Society fiscal host)
purpose: Desktop application for exploring, cleaning and transforming messy tabular data, with faceting, clustering algorithms, a transformation expression language (GREL), undo/redo history and a reconciliation framework for linking values to external identifier services.
journalism_use_case: The most accessible tool in this pillar: a reporter with no code can cluster 4,000 variant company names in a leaked spreadsheet down to 900 real entities, then reconcile them to Wikidata or a self-hosted yente instance for stable identifiers — and the operation history is an auditable record of every change made to the data.
pros: Reporters genuinely use it unaided — the clustering UI is the rare case where a statistical operation is exposed in terms a non-engineer can judge
The operation-history JSON is an underrated accountability feature: you can replay, review or publish exactly what was done to the data
Reconciliation framework is extensible, and pointing it at your own yente instance keeps identifier lookups inside the perimeter
Long-lived, institutionally stewarded and still actively developed (pushed 2026-11-17; release 3.10.1 2026-03-04)
cons: Reconciliation is the leak risk in an otherwise offline tool: it sends cell values to a web service, and the default suggestions are public endpoints — for a confidential list this is an exfiltration path hiding inside a cleaning workflow
Clustering is heuristic and over-merges distinct entities with similar names; accepting clusters uncritically creates false identities in the data
Large datasets strain the JVM heap, and the practical ceiling (hundreds of thousands of rows) is well below leak scale
No probabilistic record linkage — it clusters within a column but does not link two datasets with match weights, so Splink is still needed
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented signals: 12,109 stars, 738 open issues, continuous commits with a slower release cadence (3.10.1 in March 2026). OpenRefine's role in data journalism is long-established and reflected in its documentation and training materials; I verified no specific newsroom testimonial.
assessment: Adopt it and train reporters on it — the capability-per-hour-of-training ratio is the best in the catalogue. Then write one rule: reconciliation is disabled or pointed only at an internal yente/Wikidata mirror for any dataset derived from source material. That single control turns the tool's one serious privacy flaw into a non-issue, and it is a configuration change, not a code change.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release 3.10.1 (2026-03-04), 12,109 stars, 738 open issues. Daily commits with a slow, deliberate release cadence typical of a mature desktop application; the large backlog reflects a decade of accumulated requests rather than recent neglect.
licence_restrictions: None material. Reconciliation services you connect to have their own terms.
costs: Free. Runs on a reporter's laptop; JVM heap is the only tuning concern. No paid dependencies unless you use a commercial reconciliation service.
privacy: Cleaning and clustering are entirely local. The material exception is reconciliation, which transmits the cell values being reconciled to a third-party web service — this must be treated as a policy-controlled action for sensitive data, not a routine step.
alternatives: VisiData for terminal-based exploration of larger files
Splink or nomenklatura for cross-dataset probabilistic linkage
Datasette for sharing the cleaned result with the team

name: PaddleOCR / PP-StructureV3
purpose: OCR and document-structure toolkit covering text detection and recognition in 80+ languages, plus PP-Structure for layout analysis, table recognition and key-information extraction.
journalism_use_case: The strongest open option for Chinese, Arabic and Cyrillic document sets — a real gap in Tesseract's practical quality — and for turning scanned reports with tables into structured output on self-hosted hardware, for example Chinese corporate filings or Russian procurement scans.
pros: Non-Latin script accuracy, particularly Chinese, is materially better than Tesseract and is the specific reason to carry this dependency
PP-StructureV3 bundles layout analysis, table recognition and key-information extraction, covering a pipeline that would otherwise need several tools
Apache-2.0 code with an enormous user base (92,800 stars) and a manageable issue count (266), indicating real triage
Runs locally on CPU or GPU with pre-stageable weights, so it fits an isolated processing environment
cons: The PaddlePaddle runtime is heavier and less familiar than PyTorch; dependency conflicts and platform-specific build problems are the common complaint and cost real engineering time

Model weights were not individually verified: code is Apache-2.0 but per-model weights are distributed via HuggingFace/ModelScope and their terms need per-model checking before commercial redistribution
Last push 2026-09-16 with the latest release v3.7.0 (2026-06-11) — still recent but the slowest cadence among the leading OCR projects here
Documentation quality varies between Chinese and English versions, and the English docs lag
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: 92,800 stars with 266 open issues — one of the most-starred projects in the catalogue with evidence of active triage. The weights-licensing uncertainty is an explicit gap carried forward from session 1 and not resolved here.
assessment: Carry it specifically for CJK, Arabic and Cyrillic material, where it earns its install weight; do not make it your general OCR default over OCRmyPDF/Tesseract or Docling, because the runtime burden is not justified for Latin-script work. Before any commercial publication built on its structured output, verify the licence of the specific model weights you downloaded — that is the one open risk in this entry.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-09-16, latest release v3.7.0 (2026-06-11), 92,800 stars, 266 open issues. Two months since last push and five since the last release — slower than peers but well within normal for a 3.x line with corporate backing. Classified active, with cadence noted.
model_or_data_licence: NOT verified. Per-model weights are distributed via HuggingFace/ModelScope and were not individually confirmed as of 2026-11-17.
licence_restrictions: Code permissive. Unresolved uncertainty at the weights layer — check the specific model card before commercial redistribution. Do not assume the Apache-2.0 code licence covers the weights.
costs: No fee. CPU inference is workable; GPU is much faster for bulk. First run fetches weights (can be pre-staged). Engineering time for the PaddlePaddle runtime is the real cost. Estimate.
privacy: Local inference; first run fetches weights from HuggingFace/ModelScope, which can be done once and staged offline. No inference-time calls, so documents stay local.
alternatives: Surya or Marker for Latin-script accuracy with simpler dependencies
Tesseract via OCRmyPDF as the reliable baseline
Docling where a permissive and verified weights position is required

name: Paperless-ngx
purpose: Self-hosted document-management system that ingests scans and PDFs, OCRs them via the OCRmyPDF/Tesseract toolchain, applies machine-learning-assisted tagging and correspondent detection, and provides full-text search.
journalism_use_case: A practical self-hosted archive for a moderate corpus of source documents where reporters need reliable OCR search plus tagging without engineering support — for example a bureau's accumulated FOIA responses, court filings and leaked paperwork across years of reporting.
pros: Genuinely turnkey: a documented Docker Compose deployment gets a working searchable archive in an afternoon, which is unmatched among self-hosted document systems here
Automatic tagging and correspondent inference reduce the filing discipline required from reporters — the reason archives actually stay organised
Outstanding maintenance profile: release v3.5.0 on 2026-11-17 with only 8 open issues against 48,191 stars
Fully local with no third-party calls, and a large non-journalism user base that keeps it robust and well documented
cons: Architected around personal and office document volumes, not million-document leak triage — it will slow and become unpleasant well before leak scale
No clustering, topic discovery or entity extraction, so it organises documents but does not help you find the story inside them
GPL-3.0 affects redistribution inside proprietary tooling (irrelevant for internal use)
Its document model assumes a tidy archive of discrete documents; messy dumps with duplicates and fragments fit poorly without preprocessing
feedback: No individual user reports verified. The checkable maintenance evidence is exceptional: 48,191 stars with 8 open issues and a same-day release (2026-11-17) indicates an unusually disciplined maintainer team. No journalism-specific deployment verified; the user base is predominantly self-hosting enthusiasts.
assessment: The right answer for the newsroom-archive problem that OpenAleph and Datashare over-serve: if you need somewhere to put documents permanently and find them later, this costs a fraction of the operational effort. For your profile I would run it as the standing bureau archive and reserve Datashare/OpenAleph for individual investigations with a document dump. Do not expect it to do analysis.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release v3.5.0 (2026-11-17), 48,191 stars, 8 open issues. Same-day release and a near-empty tracker at very large scale — the strongest issue-throughput evidence in the catalogue.
model_or_data_licence: n/a — the tagging classifier is trained locally on your own documents.
licence_restrictions: GPL-3.0: distribution of a modified version obliges source release. Internal newsroom use is unaffected.
costs: No fee. Infrastructure estimate: one small VM or NAS container with PostgreSQL or SQLite plus Redis; storage proportional to document volume. Among the cheapest self-hosted options here, with low operating effort. Assumptions: Docker Compose deployment, tens of thousands of documents.
privacy: Fully local, no third-party calls, classifier trained in place. Residual considerations are ordinary server hygiene: backups contain everything, and the web UI needs authentication and TLS.
alternatives: ICIJ Datashare for investigation-scale document sets
Uwazi for public-facing collections
Mayan EDMS as an alternative self-hosted DMS with a different feature balance

name: pdfplumber
purpose: Python library built on pdfminer.six that exposes every character, line, rectangle and curve in a PDF with coordinates, plus table-detection strategies and a visual debugging renderer.
journalism_use_case: Built by a data journalist and widely used in newsrooms: character-level coordinates let you reconstruct layout-dependent documents — disclosure forms, tabular filings, court dockets — exactly, and the visual debugger makes the extraction auditable, so you can show an editor why a figure was read from a particular cell.
pros: Coordinate-level access is the capability that makes stubborn, layout-dependent documents extractable at all when generic parsers fail
The visual debugger is a genuine accountability feature: you can render exactly what the extractor saw, which makes a published number defensible
Written by and for data journalists, so the API shape matches newsroom problems (per-page, per-word, crop-and-extract)
Pure Python with a light dependency chain — easy to install, audit and run anywhere, including air-gapped
cons: No OCR: text-layer PDFs only, so scans must go through OCRmyPDF first
Table detection needs per-document strategy tuning (explicit lines versus text alignment); it is not a one-call solution at corpus scale
Slow on very large files because it models every character, which becomes a real constraint on thousand-page documents
137 open issues against 10,910 stars with the last push 2026-10-15 — healthy but single-maintainer, so response times vary
feedback: No individual user reports verified. The relevant documented context is authorship and adoption: created by a data journalist (formerly BuzzFeed News) and 10,910 stars; it is the standard recommendation in data-journalism teaching materials. I verified no specific newsroom testimonial.
assessment: Adopt it as the default PDF-extraction library for bespoke work and pair it with Camelot for ruled tables. For your profile its distinguishing value is auditability: when a story turns on a number read out of a PDF, being able to render the extraction region is the difference between a defensible figure and an assertion. Keep OCRmyPDF upstream for scans.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-10-15, latest release v0.11.10 (2026-06-15), 10,910 stars, 137 open issues. Regular point releases from a single maintainer over many years; a month since last push is normal cadence for a stable library.
costs: No fee, no infrastructure beyond Python. Cost is engineer time per document family.
privacy: Fully local, no network, no models. Suitable for air-gapped evidence handling.
alternatives: Camelot where tables have ruling lines and a confidence score is useful
PyMuPDF for speed and rasterisation — but note its AGPL licence
pypdf for simple text and page manipulation under a BSD-style licence

name: Presidio
purpose: Framework for detecting and anonymising personally identifiable information in text and images, combining NER models, regex recognisers, checksum validators and context words, with pluggable anonymisation operators.
journalism_use_case: Works in both directions, which is why it matters here: find names, national IDs, IBANs and phone numbers inside a leak to map what sensitive data it contains, and redact them before publishing documents or sharing a corpus with a partner outlet — the step that prevents a collaboration from becoming a data breach.
pros: Bidirectional utility (discovery and redaction) fits the real newsroom need: you must understand a leak's PII before you can decide what to publish
Pluggable recognisers mean you can add country-specific identifier formats (tax numbers, passport patterns) that matter for a specific investigation
Image redaction support covers scanned documents, not just text — a common gap in PII tooling

assessment: Use it as an assistive scanner, never as a redaction authority. For your profile the right pattern is: Presidio to produce a candidate list of PII locations, a human to adjudicate each one, and PyMuPDF to apply true redactions that remove underlying text. The governance transfer is worth monitoring for a release or two — the code is MIT and the community is large, so the risk is drift rather than disappearance.

privacy: Local by default and appropriate for sensitive corpora. One configuration risk: optional LLM-based recognisers would send text to a third party if enabled — review before use. Note the inherent irony that a PII tool mishandled becomes a PII exposure.
